what_it_does: Training AI models for chip-design automation (a field called EDA, or Electronic Design Automation) requires large libraries of real circuit designs as training data. However, chip companies treat their circuit files as trade secrets and will not share them, creating a data shortage that holds the field back. This paper proposes FedEDA, a system that lets companies train a shared AI model without ever exposing their circuit files to each other. Each company trains a local copy of the model on its own data and shares only the model's learned numerical weights — not the circuits themselves — with a central coordinator that averages the weights together. The key novelty is an aggregation algorithm that accounts for a mathematical principle called Rent's Rule (which relates a circuit's size to the number of external connections it needs), so that the averaging step handles the natural imbalance between small and large circuit contributions more fairly.
